editorialPolicy.storyFidelity: Each level preserves the complete event sequence, motivations, consequence, and chapter ending.
editorialPolicy.foundation: Concrete 6–11 word sentences, one main action per line, minimal subordinate clauses.
editorialPolicy.core: Connected 10–18 word sentences with cause, contrast, and reaction.
editorialPolicy.studio: Literary but speakable sentences that preserve narrator wit, suspense, and moral tension.
editorialPolicy.safety: Historic slapstick and peril are described without adding graphic detail. Harmful actions retain their consequences and are not presented as desirable.
editorialPolicy.narration: Dialogue is acted with restraint inside one continuous chapter-level performance; no independent sentence generations.

narration.direction: Let Pinocchio's promises sound eager but immature, make the crafting sequence bright and tactile, and slow down for the coat revelation so Geppetto's sacrifice lands without sentimentality.
narration.productionRule: Generate one continuous master per level and derive sentence timestamps from that same master.

livingStorybook.artBrief: A warm workshop-home panorama: unfinished wooden feet and glue on the table, Pinocchio jumping in a paper suit with bark shoes, a water bowl used as a mirror, an empty coat hook, and Geppetto returning through a cold doorway with the A-B-C book.

lines.text: Pinocchio begged for two new feet.
He promised to study and behave.
Geppetto carved and glued the feet.
Pinocchio jumped happily around the room.
Geppetto made him simple paper clothes.
But Pinocchio still needed a schoolbook.
Geppetto sold his only coat to buy it.
Pinocchio understood and hugged his father.

lines.text: After eating, Pinocchio begged Geppetto to replace his burned feet.
He promised to attend school, study hard, and care for his father.
Although he doubted the familiar promises, Geppetto's heart softened.
He carved two strong new feet and attached them with melted glue.
Pinocchio leaped around the room, delighted to stand again.
Because they were poor, Geppetto made clothes from paper, bark, and dough.
The proud puppet admired himself, then remembered he needed an A-B-C book.
Neither father nor son had any money to buy one.
Geppetto went outside and returned with the book but without his coat.
Realizing the sacrifice, Pinocchio embraced and kissed his father.

lines.text: Once his hunger was satisfied, Pinocchio immediately began to demand a new pair of feet.
He promised school, study, honest work, and lifelong support with all the confidence of a child who wanted something.
Geppetto recognized the familiar performance, yet the sight of his unhappy son softened every attempt at sternness.
With an artist's care, he carved two nimble feet and joined them so neatly that the seams almost disappeared.
The restored marionette sprang from the table and celebrated as though joy itself had entered his wooden legs.
Lacking money, Geppetto fashioned a suit from flowered paper, shoes from bark, and a tiny cap from dough.
Pinocchio admired the gentleman in his water-bowl reflection before remembering the schoolbook his promises required.
The simple request exposed their poverty, for neither of them possessed even a single coin.
Geppetto returned from the winter street carrying the A-B-C book while his patched coat had vanished.
When he claimed the day was too warm, Pinocchio understood the loving lie and covered his father with grateful kisses.
